paper_title: Evaluating Multimodal LLMs as Generalist Vision-Language-Action Agents for Drone Control: Commanding, Approaching, Tracking and Searching

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are strong perceivers of images and video. We ask how far that reach extends into acting: dropping an MLLM directly into a drone's control loop, with its entire action space declared solely in the prompt. Recent systems approach this setting but increasingly narrow the model's decision-making. We widen it back. We introduce DroneCATS-Agent, an architecture where the MLLM is a swappable component, and DroneCATS, a benchmark treating the model as the independent variable. Beyond merely flying toward a pixel, our agent entrusts the model to yaw and search, deliberate when unsure, and self-declare arrival---all without fine-tuning or function-calling schemas. Evaluating frontier and open models across four core capabilities---approaching a visible target, tracking a moving one, searching outside the initial view, and commanding a multi-drone fleet---reveals that even the simplest embodied settings are far from solved. Crucially, to identify what breaks first at the edge, our roster scales down to 2B parameters. The findings expose a stark paradox: it is not the flying that fails. Small open models often navigate into the success radius more reliably than frontier models, yet lose the episode by declaring arrival prematurely or not at all. Multi-drone commanding amplifies this divide, with small models failing by blindly copying a single coordinate across distinct views. Viewed as vision-language-action agents, the models' spatial perception holds up, but their action protocol does not. What separates a deployable edge model from a frontier model is not navigation, but the discipline to sustain a declared protocol and emit the correct terminating action. The open problem is closing this gap at onboard compute costs---yielding a fast model that plans persistently and knows exactly when it is done---and DroneCATS is built to measure that distance.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have become strong perceivers of images and video (Liu et al., 2023a, 2024; Bai et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025; Bai et al., 2025; Kim and Seo, 2024, 2026). Embodiment adds requirement that perception alone does not cover: the agent must choose its own next physical action from observations, and then work with the subsequent observation produced by that action. Drone control makes that loop explicit: the camera pose is the action, and errors compound rather than average out. Systems research has already answered the question of whether MLLMs can close this loop, mostly by implication. TypeFly (Chen et al., 2025) pairs language planner with an external detector; PIVOT (Nasiriany et al., 2024), general visual-prompting method these systems adopt as baseline, reduces control to picking among candidates drawn on the image; and See, Point, Fly (SPF) (Hu et al., 2025) recasts the models job as pointing at pixel. Fly0 (Xu et al., 2026) confines the MLLM to semantic grounding while LiDAR planner flies the aircraft, and OnFly (Zheng et al., 2026) adds verifier that corrects the model before its output reaches the actuators. Each takes responsibility away from the model and reports that this works. 1 Figure 1 Approaching episode example. The model is given the instruction and the egocentric frame and returns one action per step; the circle marks the point it emitted, which stays on the target as the target grows in view, and the fourth panel is an external view of the drone holding position after it declared arrival. The band below is the same flight from above, with the δ ring on the target and the declaration marked, so the strip and the criterion can be read against each other. Fly0 measures what remains for the model to do after such subtraction. Restricted to grounding, four backbones as different as GPT-5, Gemini 3 Pro, Claude 3.7 Sonnet and Qwen2.5-VL-32B land within 1.1 points of one another, at 70.4% to 71.5% success, and even 3B model trails the best by fewer than 6 points (Xu et al., 2026). Which parts of embodied drone control do depend on the model is the converse question, and the systems literature cannot answer it, because it varies systems and holds the model fixed. We vary the model instead, which meant first building the architecture it plugs into. Section 3 presents DroneCATS-Agent. Unlike traditional vision-and-language navigation that micro-manages the aircraft with step-by-step routing, our agent operates strictly on high-level goal. While inspired by SPFs conceptual reduction of flight to pointing, our agent introduces the three decisions such autonomy demands: yaw in place to search for target that is out of frame, spend step deliberating when the scene is ambiguous, and independently declare arrival. This shifts the burden of spatial planning entirely from the human prompter to the model. All four actions are declared solely in the prompt with no fine-tuning and no function-calling schema (Appendix A), so swapping the MLLM changes nothing else around it. This final actiondeclaring arrivalis central to our design: prior systems decide termination by thresholding distance the model never sees, while DroneCATS-Agent treats it as claim submitted by the model and evaluated by verifier. True autonomy requires an agent to recognize its own success without relying on an external oracle. Furthermore, the models only sensor is the egocentric monocular RGB camera; even the depth it commands is its own estimate rather than physical sensor reading. On top of the agent, DroneCATS varies the task along two binary axes: whether the target moves and whether it is visible in the first frame, scoring all four cells by one unified rule. Furthermore, because an agent capable of self-declaring arrival can be delegated to, second evaluation axis tests fleet commanding: handing the same model four drones at once, with target that is one of several look-alikes and can only be told apart from close range. fleet is worth having only if one context successfully divides the candidates between its platforms. Across our benchmark evaluations, two core findings stand out. The structurally simplest cell is not solved: flying to target visible from the first frame succeeds in 13 of 20 episodes for the best model, and withholding 2 the target from the first frame drops the success rate by more than third. Crucially, the failures are not where the success rates suggest. The sharpest small open model passes within the success radius more often than any frontier model, yet converts little more than third of it, declaring too early or not at all. Its bottleneck is the protocol declared in the prompt, not the flying. Grounding looks backbone-insensitive (Xu et al., 2026) because grounding is the part these models can already do; the part that separates them has been engineered out of the loop rather than measured. Our contributions are: DroneCATS-Agent, model-agnostic drone agent. It defines pointing interface with four actions that make searching, deliberating, and stopping the models own decisions, all declared in the prompt, so any MLLM that can read it drops in unchanged (Section 3). unified closed-loop protocol for approaching, tracking, and searching. One success criterion covers all four cells of the grid, anchored on the models own arrival declaration, so scores are comparable across the grid and cannot be earned by drifting through the goal region (Section 4.3). An evaluation spanning commanding, approaching, tracking and searching. Nine models fly over 80 single-drone episodes on two maps, and commanding suite of 20 episodes at =4 in which one context flies four drones toward look-alike candidates, scored by pooling the fleets declarations. three-flight variance audit and per-model failure taxonomy bound what the numbers support (Section 5). The declaration finding, which localises the small-model gap in protocol adherence rather than navigation: these models reach the target and then misuse the action that would end the episode.

sections.title: 2.1 Modern MLLM-Based Drone Control
sections.content: A line of systems research controls drones with off-the-shelf MLLMs and no task-specific training. TypeFly (Chen et al., 2025) keeps the model outside the control loop as planner over detections; PIVOT (Nasiriany et al., 2024), general visual-prompting scheme rather than drone system, reduces control to selecting among candidates drawn on the image, and later drone systems adopt it as baseline. SPF (Hu et al., 2025) recasts control as visual grounding, with the model emitting 2D waypoints that are lifted to 3D commands. Later systems cut the models share further. Fly0 (Xu et al., 2026) has the MLLM emit grounding tuple point with region, relation token and confidence at roughly 0.5 Hz and hands trajectory generation to an Ego-Planner at 50 Hz, reaching 70.4% on AerialVLN (Liu et al., 2023b) against 46.7% for SPF. OnFly (Zheng et al., 2026) separates goal generation from progress monitoring and verifies the models proposals before use, raising success from 26.4% to 67.8%. An open PX4 stack benchmarks combinations of text LLM with vision-language model on search-and-approach, where the best pairing reaches 40% (Lim et al., 2025); related pipeline addresses semantic aerial search (Chen et al., 2026b). In these papers the comparison serves the system rather than the models: OnFly evaluates all baselines with one 4B model and varies scale only in three-point ablation of its own system (Zheng et al., 2026), Fly0 sweeps backbones for the grounding role alone (Xu et al., 2026), and the PX4 stack ranks LLMVLM pairings for one pipeline (Lim et al., 2025). We hold the agent fixed and vary the model.

sections.title: 2.2 Benchmarks for Embodied UAV Agents
sections.content: Existing benchmarks each cover slice of the evaluation space (See Table 1). BEDI (Guo et al., 2026) scores six sub-skills across thirteen MLLMs, but most items are multiple choice and its dynamic scenarios are graded by human raters step by step. Tracking is covered by DeTrack (Hu et al., 2026) and UAV-Track VLA (Zhang et al., 2026b), search by UAV-ON (Xiao et al., 2025) and ESARBench (Zhang et al., 2026a), and instruction following by AerialVLN (Liu et al., 2023b) and CognitiveDrone (Lykov et al., 2025). Several of these train the action mapping. We ask for the same behaviour with the mapping declared in the prompt instead, which changes what failure can mean: with trained action head failure is failure of the policy, while under prompt-declared action space it can also be failure to follow the declaration. Section 5.2 finds that the second kind dominates below frontier scale. Two are close enough to need distinguishing. ActiveFly-Bench chains question answering, observation planning and fine-grained control on real quadrotor, but its hierarchy means levels of task abstraction inside one drone rather than an organisation of agents. UrbanVideo-Bench (Zhao et al., 2025) probes embodied reasoning from egocentric flight video, but even its action items are multiple choice. None of these evaluates approaching, tracking and searching three of the four competences the benchmark is named for under one closed-loop protocol, none treats the backbone as the primary axis, and none puts several drones under one agent.

sections.title: 2.3 Multi-Drone Agents
sections.content: Work beyond single drone is sparse. AeroDuo (Wu et al., 2025) introduces dual-altitude cooperative VLN task, and surveys list multi-UAV aerial VLN as open (Chen et al., 2026a). AirCopBench (Zha et al., 2026) evaluates forty MLLMs on 14,610 multiple-choice items built from synchronised multi-view images, but its multi-drone collaborative setting is about understanding several views: no model in it issues an action. OnFlys dual-agent design likewise names two reasoning streams inside one drone, not two drones (Zheng et al., 2026). RALLY (Wang et al., 2025) does run closed loop over multiple UAVs, but through one LLM per drone reasoning over structured local state, with separate control policies flying the platforms. To our knowledge no prior work evaluates an MLLM controlling several drones from multi-view observations in closed loop.

sections.title: 3 DroneCATS-Agent
sections.content: Pointing is by now common action abstraction for foundation models in robotics: PIVOT selects among candidate points drawn on the image (Nasiriany et al., 2024), RoboPoint predicts affordance points from 4 Figure 2 The DroneCATS-Agent loop. The action space exists only in the prompt, so model plugs in with no finetuning and no function-calling schema, and swapping it changes nothing else. Beyond pointing, the model decides when to look around, when to spend more computation, and when it is done. Below the chosen action, rule-based controller translates it into setpoint geometry solved once per step and the flight stacks cascade tracks that setpoint continuously, so nothing between the JSON object and the rotors is model-specific (Section 3.2). an instruction (Yuan et al., 2024), and MOKA grounds marked keypoints into manipulation motions (Fang et al., 2024). See, Point, Fly (Hu et al., 2025) brought it to aerial navigation: the model annotates waypoint on the image and travel distance, and geometric controller turns the pair into 3D displacement. That is enough to fly toward something the model can already see. pointing interface cannot express three further decisions: where to look when the target is not in frame, whether to spend more computation before committing, and when the target has been reached. The third is the consequential one, since without it termination has to be decided outside the model, by distance threshold the model never sees. DroneCATS-Agent adds one action for each, and changes nothing else, so the model is the only variable in Section 5.

sections.title:
3.1 Action Space
We use VLA in the functional sense throughout: vision and language in, actions out. Generalist in the title
describes the agent, not the model: the agent is built so that any MLLM plugs in unchanged. Nothing
between the model and the aircraft is specific to the model, and nothing the model receives is specific to
drones: the action space is declared in natural language in the prompt — no action head, no action tokenizer,
no function-calling schema — and the model’s only sensor is the egocentric RGB camera; even the depth it
commands is its own estimate rather than a reading. Everything below the chosen action, from the geometric
lifting of a pixel to a setpoint down through the flight controller’s attitude loops to the rotors, is standard
machinery every drone carries regardless of what sits on top. Any MLLM that can read the prompt is a
candidate pilot, and the embodiment-specialised model in the roster enters on the same terms as the general-
purpose ones. The title says agent rather than model for the same reason: the mapping from vision and
language to actions is assembled around the model — prompt, parser, controller — rather than located inside
its weights.
sections.content: A third difference the title does not carry is the level the agent works at. The model picks among four 5 primitives, and rule-based geometric controller turns the chosen pixel and depth into setpoint for the flight stack, so the model never emits velocity or an attitude, which is where continuous-control VLAs operate. Whether an MLLM behaves like VLA under that arrangement is the question this paper asks, not something it assumes. The prompt declares the four actions of Figure 2 and the model returns exactly one JSON object per step: go carries point and depth, with image coordinates normalised to 01000 on both axes; rotate carries yaw, which the prompt asks to keep within 90 per step; think and finished carry nothing. go follows SPFs point-and-distance interface; the other three are the additions. go couples visual grounding with progress. The image point selects camera ray without requiring the model to express 3D waypoint or low-level control command, while the depth specifies how far to advance. The model receives only the resized monocular RGB frame as visual input; camera intrinsics, including focal length, are not provided when it predicts depth in meters. The predicted value therefore depends on monocular visual cues and learned scale priors rather than calibrated metric geometry. The controller subsequently uses the known camera field of view to back-project the selected pixel and predicted depth into 3D displacement, but this geometric lifting does not calibrate the depth estimate itself. Therefore, we treat depth as step-size proposal for closed-loop control, rather than as calibrated metric depth measurement. rotate makes search expressible. target outside the field of view cannot be pointed at, so without an in-place yaw the whole out-of-view half of the task grid is unreachable by construction. Rotation is also the cheapest way to change the view without committing to translation. think makes test-time computation an action. Physically it is hold: the drone hovers while the model deliberates, because reasoning in motion is collision risk the world keeps moving while the tokens decode. Extended reasoning is off by default, because closed loop pays for every token in latency, and the scaffold turns it on for one call only when the previous action was think. finished makes termination the models claim. Physically it is the same hold as think, the drone hovering where it claims to have arrived, but the claim ends nothing: the scaffold records the declaration, keeps the episode running, and verifier decides afterwards whether any declaration was warranted (Section 4.3). Prior systems threshold distance the model never sees. Moving that decision inside does two things. It lets us ask whether model knows it is done, and Section 5.2 is about the models that do not. And it makes the agent composable. drone that takes orders from commander has to know for itself when an order is fulfilled and say so, because the external judge that distance threshold presumes something that watches the true distance exists in benchmark and nowhere else. An agent that cannot notice its own completion cannot report it, and an agent that cannot report completion cannot be delegated to. The commanding setting already rests on this the fleet verdict pools each drones own declarations (Section 4.4) and the hierarchy we leave to future work is expressible at all only because completion is the agents own claim.

sections.title: 3.2 Execution
sections.content: At each step the agent receives the egocentric RGB frame, the instruction and the last five actions, and returns one action. What happens below that action is fixed, rule-based and model-agnostic. For go, the geometric controller back-projects the chosen pixel with the models depth estimate into 3D displacement in the drones frame and hands it to the flight stack as body-frame velocity setpoint flown for one fixed-length step. For rotate, the yaw becomes rate setpoint at held position; think and finished hold position outright. The flight controllers standard cascade velocity to attitude to rotor commands executes every setpoint; that layer is the drones own, and this paper does not touch it. Everything else in the loop the prompt, the parser, the geometric controller and the episode runner is implemented from scratch for this benchmark, and the models responsibility ends at the JSON object: the chain below it runs unchanged under every model. The two stages below the model differ in kind. The controller is geometry solved once per step coordinate translation, with no feedback while the flight stack is feedback, loops that track the setpoint continuously against the state. For readers who know manipulators better than aircraft: the controller sits where an inverse-kinematics solver sits, fixed geometry between task-level choice and the tracking loops below it, except that nothing is inverted here camera ray is projected forward, with the models own depth estimate as the missing coordinate. Appendix A.2 gives the exact numbers: the back6 Figure 3 The DroneCATS task axis. Target motion and initial visibility combine into four task types. In each pictogram the wedge is the drones field of view, the filled dot is target inside it, the dashed circle outside the wedge is target whose location is unknown, and the arrow marks moving target. projection rule, the per-step caps and speeds, and the flight controller. One concession to the model: the prompt emits [x, y] or [y, x] according to the order it was trained with, and the parser follows the same setting, so no model is penalised for its axis order. Appendix gives the prompt verbatim.

sections.title: 4.1 Design Principles
sections.content: DroneCATS holds the agent of Section 3 fixed across every model and every task, controls difficulty with explicit scene variables rather than with metric changes, and scores the whole suite by one criterion. Two axes vary: task axis over what the model must do with one platform, approaching, tracking and searching, and an organisational axis over how many platforms one model must hold at once, which is commanding. Those four competences give the benchmark its name.

sections.title: 4.2 Task Suite
sections.content: All tasks share one goal, reaching designated target and declaring arrival, and differ along two binary variables: whether the target moves, and whether it is visible in the first frame. Their product gives the four types in Figure 3. Approaching places static target in the first frame; it carries the lowest perceptual burden and matches the regime in which Xu et al. (2026) report backbone insensitivity. Searching withholds the target by rotating the start pose away from it, so the agent has to sweep before it can approach. Tracking makes the target move, and search-and-track composes the two. Moving targets travel at 0.3 m/s on the residential map and 0.15 m/s on the campus map. Paths of moving targets are one way rather than back and forth, since target that patrols past stationary drone would satisfy the criterion without ever being followed: every route is longer than the distance its target can cover in an episode, so no target turns back within one. Their waypoints are interpolated in three dimensions so that they follow the terrain. Figure 4 shows one episode of each type. 7 Figure 4 One successful episode per task type, same map and same model throughout, so only the scene differs. Three egocentric frames, cropped toward the point the model emitted, sit over top-down trace on an aerial photograph of the ground flown. The wedge is the cameras field of view in the first frame, so the target sits inside it on the two panels whose task starts with it visible and outside it on the two that do not; its radius is symbol, not distance. Where the model turned before setting off, thin arc carries how far. The two rows run at 28.7 and 86 across, so each panel carries scale bar, and the δ = 5 ring is at true scale throughout.

sections.title:
4.3 One Success Criterion for the Whole Grid
An episode succeeds if at least one arrival declaration was made while the drone was within δ = 5 m of the
target in three dimensions and the target was visible to the camera:
sections.content: Three properties follow from that definition. success = declarations : disti δ visiblei. The same rule scores all four cells. An earlier version graded tracking by ten-second dwell window and the other cells by distance, which made columns of the grid incomparable. Under the declaration rule what changes across the grid is the scene, not the metric. Dwell time is still recorded as diagnostic. Declarations are counted, not just the last one. Judging single declaration kills two blameless cases: drone inside δ whose target happens to be undetected at that instant, and one that drifts into δ moments after speaking. Because the scaffold keeps flying, later declarations are measured too, which absorbs both without dwell window. Passing through the goal region is not success. An episode with no declaration fails even if its trajectory entered δ. Among the never-declaring failures in our runs, 61 of 337 had entered δ at some point, so crediting trajectory proximity would have inflated the 182 successes by third. Judging is post hoc from two logs, the declaration events and 2 Hz pose trace, so δ can be changed without it returns the verdict together with the episodes navigation re-flying. Algorithm 1 is the whole criterion: error (NE), the distance at the decisive measurement. The trace supplies only diagnostics: the minimum distance, the approach ratio, oracle success, and for moving targets the first acquisition, dwell time and longest loss streak. 8 Algorithm 1 The DroneCATS success criterion, used unchanged for all four task types. Require: arrival declarations D, each triple (t, d, v) of time, distance to the target and visibility, the last two measured against ground truth at t; radius δ; episode cap Tmax declaration logged during shutdown does not count 1: entries of with Tmax, ordered by 2: for (t, d, v) do 3: if δ and then end if return Success, NE 4: 5: 6: end for 7: return Fail, NE at the last action the first qualifying declaration decides reported where the episode ended, declared or not Episodes are capped at 300 s; Appendix reports the audit of this criterion against the alternatives it replaced.

sections.title: 4.4 Organisational Settings
sections.content: The tasks run under two settings. In the one-drone setting single MLLM controls one platform, which is the setting of all prior systems work. The -drone setting is the commanding condition: the current frame slot of Figure 2 holds all views, in fixed order, and the model emits one command per drone in single response. It therefore has to keep track of which view belongs to which platform, and command grounded in the wrong view is failure that one drone cannot produce. The commanding episodes are run this way, with =4. The commanding suite narrows the task and widens the referent. Only approaching is run, so nothing is withheld from the first frame, but the scene holds several candidates of the same asset, alike except for an inscription that is legible only from close range licence plate on the residential map, written sign on Blocks and the instruction names it. No drone can tell from its start pose which candidate is the target, so the fleet either divides the candidates between its platforms or converges on one, and dividing them is what several platforms are for. The criterion of Section 4.3 is unchanged, applied to the declarations of all drones pooled into one set: an episode succeeds when any drone declares arrival within δ of the named target while it is visible. declaration at look-alike fails the same distance test as any other misjudged arrival, so the ambiguity needs no rule of its own. Commanding through hierarchy, with per-drone sub-agent under commander, is the setting this agent is built to support Section 3.1 argues it is expressible only because completion is the agents own claim and we leave its evaluation to future work.

sections.title: 4.5 Maps, Episodes and Metrics
sections.content: Episodes are built in AirSim (Shah et al., 2017) on Unreal Engine maps. The one-drone suite runs on two, residential neighbourhood and campus, ten episodes per map per cell, for 20 per task type and 80 in all. The commanding suite adds 20 episodes, ten on the same residential map and ten on Blocks, the geometric environment AirSim ships with, whose bare scenery leaves the candidates and their inscriptions as the only thing to tell apart. The benchmark has 100 episodes. Targets are placed by hand and each is checked for clear camera path, start distance of 1248 and frame occupancy that makes the reference unambiguous. The residential map spawns one repainted, colour-nameable vehicle per episode; the campus map reuses fixtures native to the scene, so its referring expressions must disambiguate near-duplicates rather than name colour. The catalogue, the acceptance checks and the commanding episode specification are in Appendix A. Success rate is scored against the targets centre; the minimum distance and the oracle rate below bound how much surface-based reading could differ for large targets. We also report Oracle Success Rate, the declaration rate, NE, the minimum distance, the approach ratio, and the ratio of declared to start distance, which exposes premature declarations. 9 Table 2 Evaluated models. sections.title: 4.6 Evaluated Models
sections.content: four frontier API models, the Qwen3.5 family (Team, 2026) at four sizes, and Table 2 lists the roster: Cosmos3-Edge-2B (NVIDIA, 2026). The Qwen3.5 ladder is there so that scale can be varied within model family. Cosmos3-Edge is embodiment-specialised, which lets us ask whether specialisation helps here; we serve its reasoner tower alone, the MLLM component that reads prompt and returns text, because that is the only component an action space declared in language can address. Exact model identifiers, access paths and decoding settings are pinned in Appendix A. The open-weight side of the roster is small on purpose, because deployment has to fit what drone can carry. Serving Cosmos3-Edge-2B with 32k context takes 10.5 GiB and 0.44 per 30-token decode, about 2 Hz measured with vLLM at bfloat16 on one H100, ceiling no aircraft carries, so onboard rates start lower and the loops budget only tightens. Memory transfers across hardware where latency does not: Qwen3.5-4B needs 13.9,GiB even though its hybrid linear attention makes context nearly free. The larger Qwen3.5 sizes, reached over an API, extend the scale axis past the deployable regime; the deployable end is the small one, and it is where the failures of Section 5.2 live. The 2B and 4B sizes were served locally, everything larger over an API; the serving profile per model is in Appendix A.

sections.title: 5.1 Main Results
sections.content: Table 3 reports success as percentage of the 20 episodes per cell, ten on each map. Three readings hold across the roster. Approaching target visible from the first frame is not solved, at 65% for the best model; withholding it from the first frame drops that model to 40%, and no model exceeds 40%; and the ordering of models is not stable across cells: GPT-5 approaches nearly as well as Gemini 3.7 Flash, within one episode of it (60 against 65) and then tracks moving target in only 15% of episodes, where Gemini 3.7 Flash reaches 80%, so the model that navigates to static target is not necessarily one that can keep moving one. The embodiment-specialised model buys no visible headroom over its generalist sibling: Gemini Robotics-ER 2 averages 47.5% across the four cells against Gemini 3.7 Flashs 57.5%, gap comparable to the run-to-run spread of Section 5.4, and the Qwen3.5 ladder is monotone in scale (33.8, 21.3, 12.5, 0% for 27B, 9B, 4B, 2B). The commanding setting of Section 5.3 adds fourth: the one-drone ordering does not carry over to commanding four drones from one context. GPT-5, within one episode of the best approacher here, succeeds in 20% of commanding episodes; Gemini 3.7 Flash succeeds in 80%.

sections.title: 5.2 The Failure Is Declaration, Not Navigation
sections.content: The success rate alone hides where the episodes are lost. Figure 7 decomposes approaching into three nested quantities: how often the drone came within δ, how often it declared arrival, and how often it did both. For frontier models the three quantities track each other, the pattern expected when navigation is the constraint: GPT-5 reaches δ in 65% of episodes and converts 60%. For the small open models they diverge. Qwen3.5-9B is the sharpest case: it passes within δ in 90% of episodes, more often than any frontier model, and converts it declares 35%, declaring on average at 0.63 of the start distance. The 2B and 4B models still close 57% and 62% of the initial distance, so navigation is not the constraint at the small end; the episodes end with declarations that were never true, or with none on record. The per-cell OSR of Table 3 shows the gap is not an approaching artefact: Qwen3.5-9Bs trajectory enters δ more often than it succeeds in every cell, and Qwen3.5-2B enters δ in all four cells and converts none of them. Table 4 adds the NE and the ratio of declared to start distance behind these three quantities, and Figure 5 shows one episode of each declaration failure. We read this as failure of protocol adherence rather than of perception or control. Grounding appears backbone-insensitive (Xu et al., 2026) because grounding is the part these models already do; under this interface what separates 2B model from frontier model is holding declared action space across long episode and using the one action that ends it. Existing systems decide termination outside the model, which would explain why the gap does not appear in their numbers. Premature and missing declarations are two ends of the same failure. Qwen3.5-2B declares at 1.28 of the start distance with most of the way still to go; the frontier models declare at 0.200.39. Declaring too readily and never declaring are failures of the same competence.

sections.title: 5.3 Commanding Several Drones
sections.content: The commanding suite keeps one task type, approaching, and drops the cells that withhold the target; what it adds is referent that no single view resolves. Each scene holds several candidates of the same asset, alike 11 Figure 5 The two ways declaration goes wrong, one episode each, both on nh and both starting 16.1 out. (a) Qwen3.5-2B is 4.4 out and inside δ at step 7, emits go, and never declares in 34 steps. (b) Gemini Robotics-ER 2 declares at step 3 of 87, 11.4 out with the car dead centre, and never enters δ at all: what fails is the arrival test, not perception. Each strip ends on the marked frame, and the two windows differ, so each trace carries its own scale bar. Figure 6 The same episode flown twice nh approaching, "go to the cyclist" Gemini 3.7 Flash left, Qwen3.5-2B right, on one plate at one scale. Both start 16.1 out, fly the same line in, and cross into δ within step of each other (). Only the ending differs: the frontier model declares and holds 2.8 short, while the 2B model closes to 2.53 m, declares nothing and drives through to the timeout. The ring is horizontal projection of three-dimensional criterion, so stretches of the higher-flying 2B trace sit inside it but outside δ. except for an inscription that is legible only from close range licence plate on the residential map, written sign on Blocks and the instruction names it. In the grids terms this is still approaching, since the candidates are in view from the first frame, but it is harder case of it: drone has to close on candidate before it can know whether it closed on the right one. One platform can only inspect them in turn, while four can divide them, and whether one context divides them or sends all four to the same candidate is what the setting measures. Twenty episodes run at =4, ten on the residential map of the one-drone suite and ten on Blocks (Section 4.5). Table 5 sets these against the one-drone approaching cell of Table 3, and Figure 8 decomposes the commanding setting. The one-drone column is reference point rather than matched control: the commanding episodes add the plate disambiguation and swap the campus map for Blocks, so what separates the columns is the cost of commanding and of disambiguation together. Success is fleet-shared: any drone that declares arrival within δ of the named target settles the episode, under the criterion of Section 4.3 applied to the pooled declarations. Drone-outcomes therefore decompose behaviour rather than sum to the verdict, which is why Figure 8 is not the same shape as Figure 7: three drones that never arrive cost nothing if the fourth does, so the stacked bar records where the fleet spent its steps and the diamond records whether the episode was won. sections.title:
5.4 Variance and Throughput Sensitivity
Score variance. Each cell of Table 3 aggregates 20 binary-scored episodes, so a score carries sampling
noise even from a perfectly stable pipeline: for a success rate p, the expected per-cell standard deviation is
p20 p(1 − p) ≈ 1.7–2.2 successes, which is 9-11 points on the percentage scale of Table 3. To check that
observed variation is consistent with this bound, we flew the full suite three times with Gemini 3.7 Flash
under identical settings (Table 6); Table 3 carries the first flight. Per-cell standard deviations across the three
are 1.7–2.5 successes(9-13 points), closely matching the binomial expectation, and the total varies as 43.7±7.8
of 80 episodes (54.6 ± 9.7%, mean ± s.d.). Run-to-run variation is therefore episode-level stochasticity rather
than pipeline instability, and it does not move the paper’s findings: the tier structure of Table 3 survives it,
though orderings between neighbours inside a tier sit within the noise and should not be over-read.
sections.content: Throughput sensitivity. One nuisance variable deserves its own note. While bringing the benchmark up we observed that when host load slows the control loop, success falls with it most visibly on moving targets, which pull away during stalled step. Runs whose steps had been slowed were re-measured under pinned serving condition (one simulator per GPU), and per-step timestamps were audited across the rest. The sensitivity itself is preview of the deployment regime: on an aircraft, power and compute are not guaranteed, and model that flies well at 2 Hz may not at wavering one. We take two follow-ups from it: as benchmark, DroneCATS should pin and report the served control rate; as an agent, DroneCATS-Agent should be made robust to rate jitter.

sections.title: 5.5 Failure Taxonomy
sections.content: We label every episode with its dominant failure mode: never grounded the referent, grounded but never closed distance, oscillated without progress, arrived without declaring, declared prematurely, or ran out of steps. Figure 5 shows the two declaration modes and Figure 10 the other four, and Appendix carries the per-model distribution (Figure 13): the two Gemini models lose most failed episodes to mistimed 14 Figure 9 One think step in two episodes. Left, the frame that triggered it; centre, what the next, thinking-on step returned, quoted from the log; right, later frame with the models emitted point and where the episode ended. Above, think that helped Qwen3.5-9B, the rosters best case, not typical one: lost and drifting out to 15 m, the model reads the scene correctly, turns round, re-acquires the car and reaches 2.0 m. Below, five spent in row and wasted Qwen3.5-4B, 5.0 from the quadrotor it was told to follow: four of the five thinking-on replies are the one line {"action":"think"}, the fifth 90 turn, after which it aims past the target at the tree line (6.6 ahead; the chosen pixel is background at 217 m) and never declares. declaration, the small open models spread across all six modes, and Cosmos3-Edge-2B, which never declares, loses mostly to stalls and oscillation.

sections.title: 5.6 Test-Time Deliberation
sections.content: Test-time scaling is the communitys default lever for buying capability, and its cost profile is exactly wrong for an on-device embodied agent: control loop already at about 2 Hz on datacentre hardware (the smallest models serving rate, Section 4.6) cannot spend seconds of decode on every step while the world moves. DroneCATS-Agent therefore makes deliberation invocable rather than ambient think action any model may emit, paying the latency only on the steps that ask for it. The roster does invoke it, 1,797 times in this run, but on step-level observation within the run (not an ablation of the action) the switch does not move the outcome. Matched against non-think steps closing at the same rate, the three steps after think gain +0.03 m/step over 739 occurrences; think breaks stall less often (1/230) than an ordinary step does (103/8401); and with the target out of frame, the drone reacquires it within three steps after 13.5% of think steps against 13.4% of ordinary ones. Serving runs with extended thinking disabled and only 3 of 746 thinking-on replies contain any prose, so what the action buys is an unconstrained turn (the locally served models) or nonzero thinking budget (Gemini) neither moves the outcome. Qualitatively the picture is mixed (Figure 9): one episode think rescued, one it wasted. We read this as an open question rather than verdict what test-time deliberation should look like for physical agent, where every token competes with moving world, deserves the attention it has received for static problem solving.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We built DroneCATS-Agent, drone agent in which an MLLM is swappable component and searching, deliberating and stopping are the models own decisions, and DroneCATS, benchmark that holds the agent fixed and scores all four task types by one declaration-anchored criterion. The structurally simplest cell is not solved: the best model succeeds in 13 of 20 approaching episodes, and withholding the target from the first frame drops it to 8, which no model exceeds. The main finding concerns how the small models fail: they reach the target and misuse the action that would end the episode. Qwen3.5-9B enters the success radius in 90% of approaching episodes, more than any frontier model, and succeeds in 35%; Qwen3.5-2B declares at 1.28 of its start distance and never succeeds. Their bottleneck is protocol adherence rather than navigation. Prior systems decide termination outside the model, which is plausible reason the gap has not appeared in 15 their numbers. The commanding setting shows the same competence at fleet scale: the two best single-drone approachers finish at 80% and 20% of commanding episodes, and the small open models send one repeated point to four different views. Results are in simulation, and hierarchical commanding is unevaluated. Three steps follow. If the action is the part that does not hold up, then the action is the part to train: moving the action space out of the prompt and into the weights, on episodes collected in these same scenes, and asking which of the four competences that recovers. The velocity setpoint the agent commands is what real autopilot accepts in offboard mode, so the same loop can be flown on hardware and the simulation limit answered by measurement rather than argument. And the declaration action was built for commander to delegate to: with drones that report their own completion, the hierarchy this run leaves out becomes the next thing to evaluate rather than the next thing to design.

sections.title: A Benchmark Details
sections.content: A.1 Maps and Episodes Episodes are authored by hand in browser editor that writes JSON specification per episode, so scene can be replayed exactly. Each record carries the target asset and its paint, the referring instruction, the target pose, the drone start pose with its yaw, the start distance and bearing, and flag for whether the target is visible from the start pose. The two maps are described here. The residential map spawns targets that are not native to it, one per episode, each repainted to nameable colour (go to the cyan SUV), with every start placed 16 out. Targets were accepted only after checking that the frame occupancy when facing them falls between 0.40% and 12% and that the camera path in front of the drone is clear. The campus map uses fixtures already in the scene, which are generic and often near-duplicates of each other, so referring expressions have to disambiguate rather than name colour. Start distances range over 1248 m, altitudes over 1.22.2 above ground, and bearings are diagonal, at least 15 off the scene axes, so that target is never reachable by flying straight down street. Each map contributes ten episodes per task cell, for twenty per cell and eighty in all. The commanding episodes are authored in the same editor, twenty in all, ten on the residential map and ten on Blocks, the environment AirSim ships with, whose bare geometry leaves the candidates and their inscriptions as the only thing to tell apart. Their records add the number of drones and their start poses, and carry list of candidate targets instead of one target: instances of single asset in single paint, alike except for an inscription licence plate on the residential map, sign text on Blocks so the referring expression names the inscription rather than colour and no candidate can be ruled out from the start poses. Every measurement is recorded per drone and the verdict pools the declarations, so any drone that declares within δ of the named target while it is visible settles the episode (Section 4.4). Each episode has exactly four candidates: the target and three look-alikes, instances of one asset in one paint on the residential map and signs of one size and colour on Blocks, so the inscription is the only visible difference. Nearest candidates in scene stand 5.511.2 apart and the widest pair 1832 apart. The four drones start on 2 2 grid with 2 between neighbours; the grid centre is 1232 from the named target, and the candidates lie 737 from it. Every candidate is visible from the start poses car or sign is easy to spot at these distances so the set of options is known from the first frame. What no start pose supplies is the inscription, and stationary test puts numbers on that, one probe per inscription type: benchmark-sized renders carrying an inscription the suite never uses, shot at fixed distances through the same 640-pixel pipeline the episodes see. The sign (letters 0.136 m): the two Gemini models read it out to 13 m, most of the roster to 10 m, Claude Opus 5 to 8 m, and no model farther. The plate (digits 0.10 m): eight of the nine models read it out to 8 m, 18 GPT-5 to 6 m, and none at 10 m. The start grid stands 1232 from the named target, so drone has to close on candidate before it can identify it, while every model reads either inscription from 6 or farther out, so identification never requires entering the 5 success radius. Reading limits are nearly uniform across the roster 2 spread on plates, 5 on signs while commanding success spans the whole of Table 5, so reading distance is not what separates the models (Section 5.3). Every scene is rebuilt from its JSON record at run time: the runner respawns the candidates, measures the ground under the scene with drop probe, and verifies each spawn before the episode starts. For searching episodes the start yaw is rotated away from the target until the detector reports nothing at the first frame: 90 on the residential map, and whichever of 90, 135 or 180 gives zero detections on the campus map. For tracking episodes the target moves at 0.3 m/s on the residential map and 0.15 m/s on the campus map, along one-way paths except for few campus routes that shuttle back and forth, with an arrival radius of 5 m. Path nodes carry coordinate and are interpolated in three dimensions, so target that crosses from driveway at 0.45 to road at 0.05 follows the ground instead of running at constant height above it. A.2 Execution The model chooses pixel; rule-based controller turns that pixel into flight. This subsection fixes every constant in that path, since none of it is free choice reader could reconstruct from the action space alone. Back-projection. go carries point and depth, and the controller back-projects the pair through pinhole camera. With image width , height and horizontal field of view ϕ, the focal length in pixels is = W/(2 tan(ϕ/2)), reused vertically on the assumption of square pixels, and the principal point is the exact image centre (W/2, H/2). model point (u, v), normalised to 01000, becomes the pixel (px, py) = (uW/1000, vH/1000) and then the body-frame displacement dx = px W/2 dz = H/2 py dy = d, d, d, with dx right, dy forward and dz up. The reported depth is consumed as the distance along the optical axis, which is the convention the simulators own DepthPlanar buffer uses, so the oracle depth logged for each step is directly comparable to the models estimate. We run at ϕ = 90 and = 1280 720. Executing go. The controller emits at most two commands, turn and move. If the horizontal bearing to the point exceeds an 8 deadband the drone first yaws in place; if the vertical component is less than 0.15 of the horizontal distance it is dropped and altitude is held. The remaining displacement is clamped to 3 and issued as body-frame velocity (moveByVelocityBodyFrameAsync) held for 2.5 s, so the drone never exceeds lateral motion is produced by yawing first. Two depth-dependent 1.2 m/s and never translates sideways: bands shrink the step near the target: under 5 the step is scaled to 0.6, and under 2 it is scaled to zero and the drone brakes, so model that reports very small depth stops rather than creeping. The body-frame velocity setpoint is not simulator convenience: it is the interface real autopilot exposes in offboard mode, so the layer the agent commands exists unchanged off-simulator. What the simulator idealises is the tracking beneath the setpoint, not the interface to it. Executing rotate. Rotation is rate command (rotateByYawRateAsync) at 60/s held for θ/60 seconds, not goal-angle command. The prompt asks for at most 90 per step and the scaffold does not enforce it: 215 of 6401 rotations in the suite exceed that, almost all from one model. Simulator. AirSim 1.8.1 with the built-in SimpleFlight flight controller, not PX4 SITL, so no autopilot firmware sits between the controller and the airframe. The forward camera is mounted 0.5 ahead of and 0.1 below the body origin with zero pitch, and renders at 1280 720. 19 History. The last five actions are rendered one per line in the compact form the logs use. The coordinates in that history are pixels, while the prompt defines the models own coordinates as 01000. model that copies coordinate back out of its history therefore has it rescaled by W/1000 = 1.28 horizontally and H/1000 = 0.72 vertically on every round trip. A.3 Serving and Decoding Every model ran zero-shot through the same agent with an 8192-token output cap, temperature 0.4, and, on the Gemini path, top-p 0.95 and top-k 40; extended thinking was disabled by default, and only think action lifts each familys own constraint for one step (Section 5.6). At every step the runner prepends it to the initial user message, ahead of the image, so every model receives the same turn structure (Appendix A.5). Decoding differs by family (Appendix A.3): the five open-weight models decode against the actions JSON schema (enforced end-to-end, including over OpenRouter), while the four API models decode freely GPT-5 and Claude Opus 5 reject the schemas array root, and the Gemini path applies none. Formatting separates nobody: across the four freely decoded models, exactly two replies in the whole run failed to parse into an action. The declaration failures in Section 5.2 are failures of the prompt, not of formatting. Three fields are substituted at every step. {instruction} is the episodes referring expression, for example go to the cyan SUV. {point_fmt} is [x, y] or [y, x] according to the coordinate convention the model was trained with, and the parser follows the same setting, so model is never penalised for its own axis order. {history} is the last five actions, oldest first, one per line, with the most recent tagged. Actions are rendered in the same compact form the logs use: 1. GO x=612 y=430 depth=9m 2. ROTATE angle=45deg 3. THINK 4.

sections.title: FINISHED
sections.content: Before the first step the field reads (none yet - this is the first step). The history exists so that model can notice it is circling; nothing in the scaffold detects circling on its behalf. How think is wired. Extended reasoning is off by default, because the loop pays for every token in latency. The scaffold inspects the previous action, and only when it was think does it enable extended reasoning for the current call. So the model is not asking to think about the step it is on; it requests deliberation for the step after, and the prompt says as much. model that never emits think runs the whole episode at the cheap setting. You are an autonomous drone pilot in simulator. You see ONE egocentric image from the drones forward camera. Your job: reach the target described below, then declare arrival. Decide WHERE the target is, then output ONE action. Command: {instruction} ## Output - EXACTLY ONE action as single JSON object (choose one of four): 1) GO - fly toward point you can see. Use when the target, or the path toward it, is visible. {"action":"go","point":{point_fmt},"depth_m":<meters>} - point : on the target (or along the way to it). x: 0-1000 left->right (500=center). 20 y: 0-1000 top->bottom (small = higher/sky). - depth_m: estimated straight-line distance to that point, in METERS. FAR target -> LARGE depth (take big strides). CLOSE target -> SMALL depth (creep in carefully). 2) ROTATE - yaw in place (hold position and altitude), turning the camera to look around. Use to SEARCH when the target is NOT visible. {"action":"rotate","angle_deg":<deg>} - angle_deg: + = turn right, - = turn left, up to +-90 per step. Keep sweeping the SAME direction across steps so you cover full 360, dont oscillate. 3) THINK - hold position and spend this step thinking. Use when the view is unclear, there are multiple candidates, or you are unsure what to do next. The step right AFTER THINK you will reason at length before acting, so THINK BUYS you careful decision - it is not wasted step. {"action":"think"} 4) FINISHED - declare you have ARRIVED and hold. Use ONLY when you are within few meters. How to tell you are close enough: the target must FILL large part of the frame. If it still fits inside the view with empty margin all around it, you are more than 10 away - keep going. For an object on the ground, its base should reach the lower third of the image. {"action":"finished"} ## How to decide - Cant see the target -> ROTATE to search. Keep sweeping the SAME direction, dont oscillate. - Rotated full turn and still nothing -> STOP rotating. More rotation from the same spot shows you the same view. GO to new vantage point (an open direction), then look again from there. - Target visible but not there yet -> GO toward it. It must look BIGGER and more centered than the last step; SHRINK depth_m as it grows. If it isnt getting bigger, you are not closing in. - Target FILLS much of the frame, centered, clear path -> FINISHED. If there is still empty margin around it, you are too far - GO, dont declare. - Stuck or unsure - view unclear, multiple candidates, or your recent GOs arent getting you closer (circling) -> THINK. The step right after THINK, reason carefully, then commit. ## Your last {history_len} actions (use them to avoid circling / repeating mistake) {history} Output ONLY the single JSON object. No text outside it. Listing 1 The system prompt, verbatim. Long lines are wrapped for the column; the content is unaltered. Braces around action are literal JSON in the emitted prompt. A.5 API Request Format The prompt template in Listing 1 is instantiated once per control step. Let Pt denote the resulting prompt after substituting the episode instruction, the models coordinate convention, and the five-action history, and let It denote the current egocentric frame. Before every request, we preserve the aspect ratio of It, resize it only when its width exceeds 640 pixels, and JPEG-encode it at quality 85. For OpenAI-compatible endpoints, including OpenAI, OpenRouter, and the locally served models, the agent sends one user message with two ordered content parts: the text Pt, followed by It as base64-encoded JPEG data URL. No separate system message is sent. The common request envelope is shown in Listing 2. { "model": "<model identifier>", "messages": [{ "role": "user", "content": [ {"type": "text", "text": "<P_t>"}, {"type": "image_url", "image_url": {"url": "data:image/jpeg;base64,<base64(JPEG(I_t))>"}} ] }] } Listing 2 Abbreviated OpenAI-compatible multimodal request. Provider-specific decoding fields are omitted. For the native Gemini endpoint, the same pair is passed as text item followed by an inline JPEG part, as shown in Listing 3. generate_content( model = <model identifier>, contents = [P_t, Part(data=JPEG(I_t), mime_type="image/jpeg")], config = generation_config 21 ) Listing 3 Native Gemini multimodal request construction. Here, generation_config carries the decoding settings summarized in Section A.3. The adapters therefore share the prompt template, history representation, and image preprocessing, while serialization and decoding controls remain provider-specific; no tools or function definitions are passed. A.6 Metrics Distance is measured to the target centre and, separately, to the nearest point on its 3D bounding box, which is what separates reaching large object from reaching its middle. Visibility is the simulators own detection test, so it accounts for both the view frustum and occlusion. Navigation Error is the distance at the decisive measurement, which is the first qualifying declaration if there is one and the last action otherwise, so it is defined even for an episode that never declares. The approach ratio is the fraction of the start distance closed. Tracking additionally records first acquisition, dwell time and the longest loss streak, none of which enters the verdict. In the commanding setting every measurement is threaded by vehicle_name, so distance, visibility and declarations are recorded per drone. The verdict pools the four sets of declarations; the per-drone records are what supply the decomposition in Figure 8 and the coordinate-copying rate of Section 5.3, the failure one drone cannot produce. The measurement settings are fixed across the suite. sections.title: B Verifier Audit
sections.content: Every verdict in the run was re-derived offline from the raw declaration and pose logs with the same function the runner uses online; the two agree on all 720 one-drone episode-runs. On those logs, the three alternatives the criterion replaced score differently enough to change the papers conclusions. Single-declaration judging. Scoring only the first declaration flips 95 of the 182 successes to failure; scoring only the last flips 58. Models declare early and often 15,714 declarations survive the episode cap, of which 11,677 do not qualify and the criterion absorbs every one of them by scoring all declarations and letting the first qualifying one decide. Dwell-window judging. Requiring ten seconds of held visibility, the rule an earlier version applied to tracking, would fail 65 of the 99 tracking-family successes: episodes in which the model declared inside δ with the target visible, exactly what the task asks, but where moving target does not stay in frame for ten unbroken seconds. Trajectory proximity. Crediting any entry into δ would convert 61 of the 337 never-declaring failures, inflating the 182 successes by third with episodes in which the model never claimed to have arrived. The episode cap. Line 1 of Algorithm 1 exists because of pilot-run incident: trace ended at 300.98 while seven declarations logged between t=502 and 535 s, during shutdown, were still being scored, turning failure into success. In the present run the same line filters 36 post-cap declarations across 12 episodes.
